description: Join LimeW to collaborate on an exciting NASA Space Apps Challenge, share ideas, and build a creative solution together. We’re looking for motivated people with different skills who want to learn, contribute, and turn an ambitious idea into a strong project.
summary: Signals from the Silence is an experience that can be accessed through a web browser. It lets children between the ages of 8 and 14 play the role of Junior Deep Space Network Operators. These young learners listen in on NASA equipment that is located near the Moon on Mars and even beyond our system. Of showing complicated technical information the website makes six famous robotic explorers and tools come alive. It does this through first-person radio messages, special diagrams and short science activities that take 10 seconds to complete. The project links each spacecrafts design directly to the discoveries it helped make. It also gives a special mission patch that can be customized to celebrate completion. This project takes faraway objects and turns them into characters that students can relate to. It helps spark interest, in space exploration for the group of space explorers.
details:
What It Does and How It Works

Signals from the Silence is a browser-based game for space-loving kids aged 8 to 14. It’s about the NASA hardware still sitting on the Moon, on Mars, and out in deep space. Instead of reading about retired spacecraft like encyclopedia entries, students play Junior Deep Space Network (DSN) Operators, tuning in to signals from far away.

You pick one of three sectors (the Moon, Mars, or Deep Space) and explore six missions, some passive, some dormant, some still active. The Apollo 11 Laser Retroreflector on the Moon still works today with no batteries, and scientists bounce lasers off it to measure the Earth-Moon distance. Surveyor 3 and Apollo 12 are also on the Moon, and astronauts visited Surveyor 3 two years after it landed to see what the lunar environment had done to it. On Mars, the Opportunity Rover was built for 90 days but kept going for over 14 years, and it found hematite “blueberries” that showed liquid water once existed there. The InSight Lander listened to more than 1,300 marsquakes and used them to map Mars’s crust and liquid core. The Ingenuity Helicopter flew 72 times in Mars’s thin air, then became a stationary weather station. In deep space, Voyager 1 is still traveling beyond the heliopause through interstellar space, carrying the Golden Record.

Each spacecraft opens a DSN Telemetry Decoder, which has a radio message written in the spacecraft’s own voice, a short quiz, and a hands-on mini-lab. In the Lunar Laser Ranging Simulator, you fire a virtual laser from Earth to the Moon, see the round trip take about 2.51 seconds, and find out how far the Moon has drifted away since you were born (about 3.8 cm a year). The Space Weathering Slider lets you compare Surveyor 3’s dust and radiation damage between 1967 and 1969. In the Martian Dust-Wipe Canvas, you swipe or scratch away dust from Opportunity’s solar panels to uncover tiny hematite spheres. The Marsquake Seismograph shows a live seismograph wave and plays low seismic rumbles generated with the Web Audio API. The Thin-Air Aerodynamics Tester lets you adjust the rotor speed and see why Ingenuity needed 2,537 RPM to fly in air only 1% as dense as Earth’s. The Live Interstellar Distance Counter shows Voyager 1’s distance from Earth ticking up by the second, based on its speed of about 17 km/s.

Pass the quizzes and you unlock a personalized “Junior NASA Historian” mission patch, drawn on an HTML5 Canvas, that you can download as a PNG.

Benefits and Intended Impact

Most space mission archives are packed with jargon and tables, which can lose younger learners fast. We wanted to make planetary science feel more personal. Each spacecraft tells its own story, and each lab lets kids try something right away. The app is lightweight, needs no installation, and runs on school Chromebooks, tablets, and slow connections, so teachers can use it as a class activity. We hope it shows students how today’s retired hardware paved the way for Artemis and future Mars missions.

Creativity and Design Considerations

We didn’t want these spacecraft to feel like space junk, so we gave each one a voice and personality based on real NASA data. We focused on three things. First, making huge numbers relatable: figures like 24 billion kilometers or 1% atmospheric pressure are turned into comparisons that make sense to kids in Grades 3 to 8. Second, keeping it easy for classrooms: there’s no login and no server, the radar-style visuals are high contrast, and the controls work well on touchscreens. Third, planning for growth: the data is modular, so missions from other space agencies, like ISRO’s Chandrayaan-3, JAXA’s SLIM, and ESA’s Huygens, can be added easily.

Tools, Coding Languages, and Software Used

Built with HTML5, CSS3, and vanilla JavaScript (ES6+). The Canvas API powers the animated starfield, the dust-wipe lab, and the mission patch generator. The spacecraft diagrams are original inline SVGs, and the Web Audio API generates the marsquake sounds. We used AI-assisted code scaffolding during development, which is noted in the source metadata, and the app is hosted as a static site in the cloud.
